1:
The reforming comes after the feast, not before it, and Gill lists what had been finished first: the temple cleansed, the priests and Levites sanctified, the passover and the unleavened bread kept, and a further seven days of rejoicing. Henry makes that sequence the point. What was wanting in the preparation was made up in something better, a due improvement afterwards; when the exercises of a holy day are over we must not think the work done, since the hardest part then begins, which is to carry the impression of it into a holy life. The comfort of communion with God, he says, should kindle a zeal and an indignation against everything offensive to him — if the heart has been made to burn at an ordinance, that burning will consume the dross of corruption.

Ellicott describes the same link in plainer terms: the iconoclastic zeal of the people had been thoroughly roused by the festival they had just shared in. He identifies the objects broken — standing pillars, and the sacred trunks that served as emblems of fertility — and renders the closing phrase literally, so far as to finishing.

Three features of the destruction strike Henry. It reached beyond Judah and Benjamin into Ephraim and Manasseh. It was total, nothing spared through favour or affection, however ancient, however costly, however beautiful, however well patronised — since those who sincerely set themselves against sin set themselves against all sin. And the people would not go home until it was done, though they had been long away, being unable to think themselves safe while the images stood.

How they were able to act in the northern kingdom at all is the chapter's first real question, and the witnesses answer it four ways. Henry reports two opinions: that the cities meant had already passed under the jurisdiction of Judah's kings, or that Hoshea did not forbid the work, so their zeal carried them into his territory. He adds a third possibility, that the northerners who had come south for the passover went home and destroyed their own images, persuading as many others as they had influence with to allow the same. Clarke declines to choose — whether it was a transport of religious zeal or was done with Hoshea's consent, he says, we cannot tell. Wesley is definite on both counts: the people acted by a special impulse of the Spirit, and Hoshea, who contented himself with the calves and did not practise the grosser idolatry of his predecessors, would patiently suffer the images of Baal to be broken.

Ellicott answers from politics rather than piety. The northern kingdom was by this time in the last stage of weakness and drifting fast toward ruin, so a band of zealots drawn from both nations was unlikely to meet serious resistance. Clarke, surveying the chapter as a whole, treats the episode as the first of a series: the traces of idolatry destroyed, the state of religion reformed, the tithes brought in from every quarter with officers set over them, the priests and Levites regulated by their genealogies, and the king prospering because he did all of it in sincerity and truth.
2:
With the images down, the king turns to organisation. Gill notes that the courses had been fixed by David, were still running in Jehoshaphat's day, had since been interrupted, and were now put back in their regular order; Ellicott says the same in a phrase, that Hezekiah restored the rotation ascribed to David. Delitzsch adds the detail of proportion — each man was set according to the measure of his service — and divides the work as the verse does, priests for the burnt offerings and the thank offerings, Levites to wait upon the worship and to praise with song and instrument.

Henry draws a rule out of the arrangement. The service was put into its proper method again, to run in the old channel, and every man was made to know his work, his place, his time and what was expected of him; good order, he observes, contributes much to the carrying on of a good work. He assigns the Levites two branches, some ministering to the priests and others giving thanks and praise.

The phrase that calls the temple a tent draws three different explanations. Delitzsch renders it the camp of the Lord and takes it for the temple with the court of the priests. Clarke is content that it means the temple simply, that building being house and tabernacle and tent and camp of the Most High at once. Henry hears something more pointed in the word: the temple is called a tent because the privileges belonging to it were movable things, and this temple in particular was shortly to be taken away.

Then the funding, which the witnesses treat as the reform's substance rather than its trimming. Gill explains that the king gave out of his own treasury, of his royal bounty, beyond what kings usually supplied for their own sacrifices — the temple treasury being exhausted and the people left poor by the previous reign. Clarke reports the conjecture that the kings of Judah had from David's time furnished the morning and evening sacrifice daily at their own charge. Delitzsch simply identifies what was given: the material for the burnt offerings the law commands, drawn from the royal possessions. Henry states the principle he sees at work — the people were liable for the daily offerings and those of the sabbaths, new moons and feasts, but rather than see them burdened the king met the cost from his own estate.

The command to the people follows, and Ellicott notes that it is put quite plainly, that the king said to the dwellers in Jerusalem to give the portion. Gill and Ellicott agree on what the portion was, the tithes and firstfruits the law had already assigned. Delitzsch explains the purpose clause, and it is the most practical sentence in the section: the priests and Levites were to be maintained so that they might hold firmly to the law, giving themselves to the duties it laid on them without being driven to work for their own subsistence.
5:
The command travelled faster than the king can have expected. Gill notes that it was not merely published in the capital but carried through the cities of Judah, and observes that the same is true of the verse about the country dwellers, where he thinks the supplied word concerning can be dispensed with — Ellicott would strike it out too. What came back was firstfruits of corn, wine, oil and honey, and the tithe of everything the fields produced. Clarke identifies the purpose these were principally for, the maintenance of the priests and Levites, and Delitzsch divides them more exactly: the firstfruits belonged to the priests, the tithes to the whole tribe of Levi.

Delitzsch makes two further points about who gave and what was given. The children of Israel named here are not the population of the northern kingdom but Israelites who had emigrated south into Judah. And the phrase about a tenth of holy things surprises him, since the law does not speak of a tenth of consecrated gifts but only of heave offerings taken from them — a difficulty he records rather than smooths away.

The dating occupies the rest of the passage, and the witnesses agree on the months while differing on what the months meant agriculturally. Gill identifies the third as Sivan, the month of Pentecost, and puts it at the point where barley harvest ended and wheat harvest began. Ellicott gives the same month, answering to our May and June, but places it at the close of wheat harvest rather than its opening. Delitzsch says simply that the heaps were begun immediately at the end of the grain harvest. Wesley, more broadly still, has the third month as the one in which their harvest began and the seventh as the one in which it ended.

About the seventh month there is no such divergence. Gill's Targum and Clarke both name it Tisri; Ellicott dates it to September and October and marks it as the month of the great Feast of Tabernacles, kept when every fruit had been gathered and the vintage was over; Delitzsch describes the heaps as completed at the end of the fruit and wine harvest. So the piling ran from one pilgrim feast to the other, a full agricultural season. Ellicott notes in passing that the verb translated as laying a foundation takes a curious form found only here, and Clarke explains what the heaps physically were — the vast collections of grain the tithes produced over and above what the givers themselves consumed.
8:
The king came to look at what had accumulated, and what he did first was bless. Gill identifies the heaps as the tithes and firstfruits; Delitzsch records that Hezekiah and those with him praised the Lord and his people Israel — the gift and the givers both acknowledged. Then he asked a question, and Delitzsch is careful about what kind of question it was. Hezekiah was not enquiring whether the stores would be enough to maintain the priests and Levites; he wanted to know how such masses had come to be heaped up at all. Gill allows a second possibility alongside it, that the king was asking why the heaps had been left lying where they were.

Who answered is disputed. Gill identifies Azariah as high priest of the family of Eleazar in the line of Zadok, the line raised to the office in Solomon's day when Abiathar was thrust out, and passes on Jarchi's view that this is the same Azariah who served under Uzziah. Delitzsch thinks that hardly possible, since the man who confronted Uzziah in the holy place did so some forty years earlier. Ellicott holds the identification open — possibly the same, and if not, then a man otherwise unknown.

The answer itself is a sentence the commentators enjoy. Delitzsch notes that the Hebrew uses infinitives absolute where ordinary speech would use a plain past tense, and puts the effect down to animation — the priest is not reporting but exclaiming. Ellicott renders the construction literally as eating and being satisfied and leaving over, even unto abundance, and reads the clause about the Lord blessing his people as the explanation of the surplus: they had been able to give liberally because they had been given much.

Ellicott adds two smaller notes on the same verses. The word for what the people brought is the one usually rendered heave offering, and it appears here in a contracted form found in only one other place. And what is described as left over is what remained after the priests' own maintenance had been subtracted, which is the point of the whole exchange: the surplus was not the provision, it was what the provision had not needed.
11:
The surplus had to be housed, and Gill notes that it is not clear whether new chambers were built or existing ones fitted up. Henry treats the decision as the first of two instances of the king's care for matters he had already set in order. The stores were not to be left in loose heaps, open to waste and embezzlement, but laid up in rooms in the temple courts and kept under lock and key, with treasurers appointed to see that neither moth and rust corrupted them nor thieves broke in to steal. Henry draws the lesson from the ant that provides her meat in summer, and adds a shrewd observation about giving: laying the surplus up safely encouraged the people to keep paying in, since the public gives cheerfully to what it can see is well husbanded.

His second instance is the balancing one. Church treasures are not to be hoarded any longer than there is occasion for them, lest the very rust become a witness against those who hoard; so officers were appointed — men, Henry has no doubt, of approved wisdom and faithfulness — to distribute what had been gathered. Storing and spending are two halves of the same trust.

The men themselves are named, and Delitzsch sorts out the hierarchy. Cononiah the Levite was set over the stores with his brother Shimei second to him, and ten more Levites served beneath them as subordinate overseers; fourteen in all had the keeping of the firstfruits, tithes and dedicated things, while separate officers were appointed for the distributing. He identifies the Azariah named alongside the king as the high priest who had answered him a few verses earlier, and prefers to render the phrase about royal authority as by the mandate of Hezekiah.

Gill and Ellicott fill in around that. Gill stresses the word faithfully: nothing was kept back for private use, the whole of what came in being delivered up and stored. He describes the ten as assistants under the command of the first two, ready at hand for whatever they were directed to do, and Ellicott agrees that the phrase means precisely under Cononiah's orders. Ellicott admits that nothing is known of these ten beyond their names, two of which appear elsewhere, and notes that the word rendered commandment carries an unusual sense here, since it ordinarily means a census.
14:
Distribution was a separate office from storage, and it had its own chief. Gill identifies Kore as the porter at the east gate of the temple. Delitzsch and Ellicott agree on his charge: the freewill offerings, the voluntary gifts, which he was to distribute along with the oblations and the most holy things. Six Levites worked under him, and Ellicott renders the phrase describing their position as by his hand, meaning subordinate to him.

Where those six operated is the one point on which the witnesses pull apart. Gill takes Kore's own business to have lain chiefly with the priests in the temple and in the capital, and the six under him to have been employed in distributing to the priests. Ellicott places them out in the priestly cities themselves, stationed where they served, handing out a proper share of firstfruits, tithes and dedicated things to the brethren living there. Delitzsch reads it the same way, and explains who those brethren were: not only the Levites resident in the priests' cities who through youth or age could not come up to the temple, but also the men whose course was not on duty at the time, since the courses served by turns and most were at home in any given week.

Two smaller readings attach to the same verse. Ellicott would connect the phrase about their set office with the verb that follows rather than with what precedes, giving the sense honestly to give, and glosses the pairing of great and small as simply older and younger. Clarke records a variant in one of the six names, where several manuscripts and the ancient versions read a more familiar form. Wesley sums the office up without complication: these men were entrusted with receiving the portions belonging to the priests and with handing them on.

The age at which a claim began interests Gill most. The register ran from three years old and upward, and he gives Kimchi's reasons for the threshold — below that age a child was not fit to come into the temple, had not the understanding to keep what was put into his hands, and might defile an offering by handling it, whereas at three he could begin to be taught how to hold such things. Females, Kimchi adds, were not admitted at any age.
17:
A parenthesis interrupts the account of the distribution, and Ellicott explains why it is there: the word register in the preceding line has drawn the writer aside into a note about how the registers themselves were kept. He would translate it as a statement in two halves — the roll of the priests was made out by clans, and the Levites from twenty years old upward stood in their offices by divisions. Gill reads the same verse as recording that a portion was given to priests and Levites alike once they were entered in their family registers at the appointed age.

Then the roll widens to take in households. Gill notes that wives and children were genealogised too, sons and daughters, small and grown alike, and that the portion was distributed according to the number in each family. Delitzsch finds the verse genuinely hard. Read as a continuation of what precedes it, he says, it yields no suitable sense; one proposed supplement he rejects as arbitrary, and another scholar's suggestion about where the thread resumes he accepts while rejecting that scholar's rendering of the key word. His own solution comes from the following verse, where the same construction appears in a context clear enough to fix its meaning. Ellicott reaches the same structural conclusion more briskly, that after the two parenthetic statements the narrative picks up again where it had been broken off.

The last of the three verses extends the provision to the countryside. Gill describes the fields of the suburbs as the lands allowed the priests out of the several tribes, where they lived when their course was not on duty at the temple, and insists that these men received a portion for themselves and their families as much as those in the capital did. Delitzsch adds that in each such city men were appointed and named expressly for the work of giving out portions to every male among the priests and to all who stood registered among the Levites. Ellicott extends the reach one step further, to the priests and Levites living out on their farms beyond the sacerdotal cities altogether. Between them the three witnesses describe a system that followed the ministry home rather than making it come to town to be paid.
20:
The account closes with a verdict, and the witnesses spend their attention on the three words it uses. Gill summarises the king's actual achievement first — the courses of priests and Levites settled, and a provision made for them and their households. Delitzsch marks the verse as the conclusion of the whole narrative, and paraphrases its second half: in every work Hezekiah began for the service of the house of God, and for the restoring of the law and its commands, he sought his God, did it with all his heart, and prospered.

Clarke turns the three terms into a portrait of what a king ought to be. He is good, and does good; he is upright, and acts justly and maintains justice; and he is truly religious, living according to the truth he has received as a revelation from God. Ellicott glosses the third word more narrowly, as faithfulness or sincerity, which keeps the sequence moving inward — from what the king did, to how he did it, to what he was.

The final verse repeats the point with a change of emphasis, and Gill lists what the works actually were: cleansing the temple, providing the sacrifices, placing the priests and Levites in order, taking care of their maintenance. Nothing in that list is spectacular. It is administration, and the chapter's judgement falls on the spirit in which the administration was carried out.

Ellicott keeps close to the Hebrew here. The word for commandment stands in the singular; the phrase about seeking God is better read as in order to seek, or by way of seeking, so that the whole enterprise was itself an act of seeking rather than a condition for it; and the expression with all his heart he sets beside the familiar language of serving with a perfect heart and of loving God with the whole heart. Clarke ends where the chapter does, calling Hezekiah in every respect a thoroughly excellent man who saw his duty to God and to his people and performed it with becoming zeal and diligence — and then breaking into a wish, that God would always send such kings to the nations, and that people blessed with them would be duly obedient and thankful for it.
